# Double-entry bookkeeping (`double_entry`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by arabic_numerals
- Core idea: Each transaction has equal total debits and credits across at least two accounts (receiving 100 florins from Piero: debit Cash 100, credit Piero 100). Keep a dated journal of all transactions and a ledger with one page per person, good, cash and the owner's capital. Because every entry has two equal sides, total debits must equal total credits; a trial balance that does not agree shows an error at once. At year end the accounts are closed into a profit-and-loss account and a balance, which tells the owner his profit per venture, what he owes and is owed, and lets a partner or auditor check a distant agent.
- Pitfalls:
  - Taking balanced books for honest books: an omitted transaction or a fraud entered on both sides balances perfectly
  - Saying Pacioli invented it: he described in print (1494) a Venetian practice already some two centuries old
  - Reading debit and credit as bad and good, or as minus and plus everywhere: their sign depends on the kind of account
  - Mixing the owner's household spending with the business, or valuing stock differently each year, makes the profit figure meaningless
  - Claiming double entry created capitalism (Sombart): historians such as Yamey argue merchants decided without it and many prospered with single entry
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2100–2000 BC – Ur III scribes balance receipts against issues for each official, a careful single-entry control, not double entry; china: Song onwards – 'four pillars' (sizhu) method: opening balance plus receipts minus issues equals closing balance; Qing merchants' longmen zhang is sometimes called double entry, the claim is disputed; islamic: Abbasid to Ilkhanid state accounting kept elaborate balanced registers (al-Mazandarani's manual, 1363); claims that true double entry began in the Islamic or Cairo Geniza world are disputed; europe: c. 1300 – earliest surviving double-entry ledgers of Tuscan firms (Farolfi company, 1299–1300); 1340 Genoa's communal treasury (massari) ledgers in full double entry; 1458 Cotrugli's manuscript Della mercatura describes it (printed 1573); 1494 Luca Pacioli's Summa, first printed treatise; east_asia: Kaesong merchants of Korea used a four-element double-entry system (sagae chibubeop); its origin before the 18th c. is unproven
- Read:
  - Luca Pacioli, Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalita (1494)
  - Jacob Soll, The Reckoning: Financial Accountability and the Rise and Fall of Nations (2014)
  - B. S. Yamey, Scientific Bookkeeping and the Rise of Capitalism, Economic History Review 1 (1949)
